Henry Boynton Smith
hen'rē boin'tən smith
n. (Henry Boynton Smith, 1815–1877, New School Presbyterian theologian at Union Theological Seminary, New York)
English occupational surname Smith, a worker in metal.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Henry Boynton Smith was converted out of Unitarian Maine, studied at Halle and Berlin under the German mediating theologians, and taught church history and then systematic theology at Union Seminary in New York for twenty-four years. He belonged to the New School party and worked to heal its breach with the Old School, which was accomplished in 1869; his address on Christian union was the instrument. His System of Christian Theology, published from his lectures after his death, organises doctrine around the incarnate Christ as the centre of all revelation and history. He held the Reformed doctrines of election and atonement while recasting them in a christocentric frame learned in Germany, and he translated and introduced much German theology to American readers. Col 1:28 describes the aim, Eph 1:4 the doctrine he would not surrender, that God “hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a system as a connected scheme of principles or doctrines, and union as the junction of two or more things into one.

expand to see more

SYS'TEM, n. An assemblage of things adjusted into a regular whole; a connected scheme or body of doctrines.

UN'ION, n. The act of joining two or more things into one, and thus forming a compound body or a mixture; concord; agreement.

MEDIA'TION, n. Interposition; intervention; agency between parties at variance, with a view to reconcile them.

Key Scripture

Col 1:28 — "Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:"

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

1Co 1:10 — "Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment."

Act 20:30 — "Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them."

Modern Corruption

A German-trained New School theologian who held election and spent himself on reunion.

expand to see more

Smith is the best case for the New School and shows both its strength and its hazard. The strength is that he kept the substance: Eph 1:4 as unconditional choice before the foundation of the world, and an atonement that actually satisfies. The hazard is the frame. A christocentric reconstruction learned from the German mediating school tends to treat doctrinal formulations as expressions of a central life rather than as propositions to be defended, and that habit, passed to the next generation, dissolved what Smith himself held.

The reunion of 1869 was accomplished on terms that did not settle the doctrinal questions of 1837, and Act 20:30 warns where the cost falls: “of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things” (Act 20:30). The dictionary values 1Co 1:10 and the labour for unity, and holds that unity which postpones the doctrinal question postpones it to a generation less able to answer it. Union Seminary's own course after Smith is the demonstration.

Usage

"“hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4) — what he would not give up."

"“that there be no divisions among you” (1Co 1:10) — the labour of his later years."

"“of your own selves shall men arise” (Act 20:30) — where a postponed question goes."
